item.title: Marcus Junius Brutus: Rome's Most Notorious Traitor
item.description: Marcus Junius Brutus is alternately remembered as a noble man who acted in opposition to tyranny or as one of the most notorious traitors in history. Said to have been descended from the semi-legendary founder of the Roman Republic, Brutus came to oppose the autocratic behavior shown by Caesar after the latter became dictator. Brutus and the other conspirators decided to attack Caesar at a Senate meeting, which would be held at the Senate House in the Portico of Pompey on the Ides of March.

item.title: Battle of Passchendaele: Haig's Folly in the Mud of Flanders
item.description: The Third Battle of Ypres was widely seen as an Allied failure. Strictly speaking, Haig had won the battle, but the gains were minimal and the costs high. item.title: Scribes in Ancient Mesopotamia: The Beginning of History
item.description: Scribes in Mesopotamia were initially tasked with recording transactions in trade and keeping records. Eventually, they became an integral part of everyday life and were involved in trade, royal correspondence, record-keeping at the temple complex, military matters, long-distance correspondence, construction of new buildings, and agricultural concerns, among many other tasks. They also composed original compositions and, essentially, created what we know as history.

item.title: The Barracks Emperors: Instability of Populist Rule
item.description: Throughout the Crisis of the Third Century, there were over 20 barracks emperors who rose quickly to power and, in many cases, were dispatched just as fast. Even a man who would have been an able and acceptable emperor in another time might be found wanting in this period, and there was no margin for error in how an emperor comported himself or led military campaigns. Any sign of weakness or ineffectuality could be considered just cause to remove an emperor and replace him with a better.

item.title: German Spring Offensive: Ludendorff's Last Chance to Win WWI
item.description: The German Spring Offensive, also called the Ludendorff Offensive after its commander, was the last major German advance of the First World War (1914-18). From March to July 1918, Ludendorff launched five major attacks on the Western Front to break the deadlock of trench warfare. item.title: Antinomian Controversy: Inspiring the Separation of Church and State in the USA
item.description: The Antinomian Controversy (1636-1638) was a religious-political conflict that divided the Massachusetts Bay Colony of New England. The disagreement centered on the primacy of God's grace over good deeds, but it was actually about the challenge to the Boston magistrates' civil authority over religious matters and the colony's unity of vision. item.title: Gaius Cassius Longinus: Liberator, Tyrannicide, or Traitor?
item.description: Gaius Cassius Longinus - though his name is not as famous as that of Brutus, he is forever linked with the assassination of Julius Caesar on 15 March 44 BCE. From the ancient sources, like Plutarch, to the works of William Shakespeare, his story and motivations have long been discussed. Was he a traitor who murdered Caesar to get ahead? Or a defender of Roman liberties, martyred for his cause? Cassius's story is an interesting one, one that has echoed down the long centuries to reach us today.

item.title: Mesopotamian Education: Creating the First Written Works in History
item.description: In ancient Mesopotamia, students seem to have begun their education as early as the age of eight, attended class from sunrise to sunset for at least 24 days a month (possibly year-round), and graduated in their early twenties as scribes. Schools also had large ceramic vessels that held damp clay, which would be molded into writing tablets, and others filled with water into which old tablets were dropped to soften so they could be erased, reformed, and reused.
